name: Priya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. All right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Perfect. I'll warn you, I talk fast and I'll probably show you something on my phone at some point. Ask me to slow down if I get carried away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the field and livestock lead at Oakfield, a 250-hectare organic farm owned by a community land trust. Mornings I check the outdoor pigs and the sixty dairy cows with the herd team, then I'm in the veg fields planning harvest for our box scheme, which feeds about 900 households. I use an AI assistant every day, for the crop rotation, the irrigation timings and the weekly newsletter to box customers. What wears me out is the meetings, honestly, because a trust has a lot of opinions.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leo is a software tester for an insurance firm, mostly from home. We've got Amara, who's eleven, and Zain, who's eight, and a mortgage on a semi in the market town. We're comfortable, more than a year of savings plus some shares Leo's been buying for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I think the tools have more in them. At the trust I'd say keep using what works, like the irrigation planner. Online I'd probably post something nerdy about soil sensors that nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means very little changes. My job is safe, the trust values people, and Leo's testing work carries on. I'd still spend Thursday nights asking an AI to write the veg box newsletter, and nobody at Oakfield would be any worse off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep pushing the small tools that save time. This winter I'd trial an AI pest-alert service on the brassicas, which costs about three hundred a year. Otherwise we'd carry on saving and maybe do the trip to see Leo's family in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. I like change, so a world where nothing much happens is slightly boring for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already pressing on you, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust's budget is always tight, because organic veg margins are thin and the pig price swings. But the members are loyal and there's a waiting list for veg boxes. If I'm honest, my pressures are mostly about time, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a world where nothing happens is boring. Would you push more AI onto the farm anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently, yes. The herd team would grumble, especially Graham, who's been milking for thirty years and thinks the phone is a fad. I'd only bring in what saves him effort, otherwise it's just me playing with toys.

say: I'd say I'm **disappointed**, because the tools have more in them.
I'd tell the trust to **keep using what works**, like the irrigation planner.
think: My **job is safe** and the trust values its people.
Leo's **testing work** carries on, so the household is steady.
do: Trial an AI pest-alert service on the brassicas for about **£300 a year**.
Keep **saving** and plan the spring trip to Leo's family.
feel: Calm and a little **flat**, because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: I'd still spend Thursday nights asking an AI to write the veg box newsletter, and nobody at Oakfield would be any worse off.
fieldNote: Priya is a **daily AI user** who is mildly bored by a no-change world.
Her pressures are **time and meetings**, not money.
She is careful not to push tools on **Graham**, the veteran milker.

steps.text: Trial an AI pest-alert service on the brassica crop
Keep running the veg fields and herd checks as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good for farming, because the paperwork and the planning get easier. I'd also say the gains should go to the people doing the work, not to three tech firms. At the trust I'd push us to share what we learn with other small farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is fine, but Leo's isn't. Software testing is exactly the checking and coding work this picture says goes first. My job on the farm is the safe one in our house now, which nobody would have guessed ten years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Leo this month and look hard at his options, maybe moving into testing farm robots or the sensors I use. We'd put a bit more into savings while he's still on full pay. At Oakfield I'd bring in an AI system for the box scheme orders, which would free up a day a week for Marta in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for Leo, excited for the farm. It's an odd mix, cheering at work and then coming home to a quiet kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd free up a day a week for Marta. What happens to Marta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd want to get right. Marta's brilliant with customers, so I'd want that day to go to her running the farm shop, not to a cut in her hours. At a trust we can decide that together, which is the whole point of being a trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if Leo's pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car and the eating out, easily. We wouldn't touch the kids' activities, Amara's swimming and Zain's football. We have the cushion, so it's not about survival, it's about not draining it while he works things out.

say: I'd say it's **good for farming**, because paperwork and planning get easier.
I'd say the gains should go to **workers**, not three tech firms.
think: My farm job is fine, but **Leo's testing job** is exactly what goes first.
The farm job is now **the safe one** in our house.
do: Sit down with Leo **this month** to plan a move into farm-tech testing.
Put **more into savings** while Leo is still on full pay.
Bring in **AI ordering** for the box scheme and move Marta to the shop.
feel: **Worried for Leo**, excited for the farm.
S1.quote: My job on the farm is the safe one in our house now, which nobody would have guessed ten years ago.
fieldNote: Her own job is secure; the risk is to a **household earner**, Leo.
She treats automation as a **trust decision** about where freed time goes.
Strong savings make this about **not draining** the cushion, not survival.

steps.text: Help Leo plan a move into testing farm robots and sensors
Raise monthly savings while Leo is on full pay
Bring in AI ordering for the 900-box veg scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public rules right now, before a handful of companies own every robot. At the trust I'd say we have to own our machines, not lease them. Online I'd be sharing things about public ownership of AI, which my sister would roll her eyes at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, Leo's job is gone in 2028, and probably most of mine by 2031. The trust might keep me on to run the robots, but a robot doesn't need a field lead. I'd be the person teaching the robot my own job, then hoping Oakfield still needs a human to switch it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away we'd stop overpaying the mortgage and keep the cash. I'd put a proposal to the trust: any money robots save goes into a fund for staff, and people retrain on full pay. I'd learn the machines faster than anyone, because the person who understands them stays longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly at night. During the day I'd be busy and nearly enjoying it, which makes me feel a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. How does that split land on your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning half of my job goes in 2028: rotations, ordering seed, the box scheme forecast. I'd still be needed in the field for three years, so I'd become the hands for the AI's brain. Then in 2031 even the hands go, unless the trust decides it wants people anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amara and Zain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth in small pieces, that Dad's job is changing and Mum's is changing too. Amara would ask straight away if we're poor now, because she's that kind of kid. I'd tell her no, we've saved, and that we'll be fine for a long while.

say: I'd demand **public rules now**, before a few firms own every robot.
I'd tell the trust to **own our machines**, not lease them.
think: **Leo's job is gone** in 2028, and most of mine by 2031.
The trust might keep me to **run the robots**, but that's a hope.
do: Stop **mortgage overpayments** and hold the cash.
Propose a **staff fund** at the trust from robot savings, with paid retraining.
Learn the **farm robots** faster than anyone else at Oakfield.
feel: Scared **at night**, busy and nearly enjoying it by day.
S2.quote: I'd be the person teaching the robot my own job, then hoping Oakfield still needs a human to switch it off.
fieldNote: She expects **both household incomes** to go or shrink within three years.
Her adaptiveness turns into a bet: **understand the machines** to stay longest.
Progressive instincts go straight to **ownership** of the robots.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the mortgage and keep the cash
Propose a staff fund at the trust from robot savings
Learn to run and repair Oakfield's farm robots first
Explain the job changes calmly to Amara and Zain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this fairly if we start this year. I'd be pushing our MP on public ownership of farm robots, and I'd get the trust writing to other land trusts. At the school gate I'd be the annoying optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still tough on Leo, but five years means he can move before 2031. My hands-on work lasts until about 2034, so I'd have eight years. I think I could make myself the person who runs the robots for three or four farms in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an agricultural robotics course next autumn, one day a week, which the trust would pay for. Leo would move into testing farm machines, and we'd use our savings to cover a pay cut if he needs one. At Oakfield I'd start trials with a robot weeder in the carrots by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot in my stomach. It's a race, but I think it's one I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the warning time change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns panic into a plan. In the fast one I'm learning on the job while it's happening. With five years' warning I'd stop being a farmer who uses robots and become the woman who runs them for the whole valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the annoying optimist'. Is there a part of this you're not optimistic about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The politics. I can plan my own life, but I can't make the government share the gains. If it all goes to the people who own the robot companies, then my clever plan just means I'm the last one standing in a very empty valley.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do this fairly if we start now.
I'd lobby **our MP** on public ownership of farm robots.
think: Leo can **move before 2031**, and I have eight years of hands-on work.
I could run **robots for several farms** in the valley.
do: Start an **agricultural robotics course** one day a week, paid by the trust.
Use savings to cover Leo's **pay cut** while he moves into farm-machine testing.
Run a **robot weeder trial** in the carrots by 2028.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with a knot in her stomach.
S3.quote: With five years' warning I'd stop being a farmer who uses robots and become the woman who runs them for the whole valley.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **panic into a plan** for both earners.
She still expects income change, but with **real control** over it.
Her doubt is **political**: who gets the gains.

steps.text: Take an agricultural robotics course one day a week
Run a robot weeder trial in Oakfield's carrots by 2028
Write to the local MP about public ownership of farm robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the three, and we'd be fools not to use it. I'd want the trust to become a model farm for how robots and people share the work. I'd be talking about it to anyone, the vet, the feed rep, the box customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd come out of this one well. Leo has years to switch, I'd have more than a decade before the hands-on work goes, and by then I'd be fifty-six and know these machines inside out. My worry is everyone else, the farms that can't afford to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a ten-year plan for Oakfield with the board and start the first robot trials by 2030. We'd put some savings into a farm-robotics co-op that some friends are setting up, a small stake, maybe five thousand. And I'd keep lobbying for a public fund to help small farms buy shared machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, and a bit excited. Uneasy only when I think about the farms down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Graham, the milker you mentioned, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham's sixty-two, so by 2039 he's long retired, and I'm glad. In the faster ones I'd lie awake about him. In the slow picture our old milker Graham gets to retire on his own terms, and that matters more to me than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd come out well. Is there anything that could knock that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trust ran out of money, or if the big firms priced small farms out of the machines. I can't control that. But with ten years' warning I'd have built enough of a name that another farm would hire me.

say: I'd call this the **best of the three** and say we'd be fools to waste it.
I'd want Oakfield to be a **model farm** where robots and people share work.
think: I'd come out **well**, knowing the machines inside out by fifty-six.
My worry is **smaller farms** that can't afford to adapt.
do: Draft a **ten-year plan** for Oakfield and start robot trials by 2030.
Put about **£5,000** into a friends' farm-robotics co-op.
Lobby for a **public fund** to help small farms share machines.
feel: Calm and **a bit excited**, uneasy only about neighbouring farms.
S4.quote: In the slow picture our old milker Graham gets to retire on his own terms, and that matters more to me than any robot.
fieldNote: A decade's warning makes this **good news** for her own work and household.
Her concern shifts to **other farms** and colleagues like Graham.
She'd take a small, **personal stake** in a robotics co-op.

steps.text: Draft a ten-year robot plan for Oakfield with the trust board
Buy a £5,000 stake in a farm-robotics co-op
Lobby for a public fund for shared farm machines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Leo and I would both be changing at once, with two kids and a mortgage. What would help is paid retraining that doesn't wait for you to be out of work first. And rules so the trust can own its robots instead of renting them forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel responsible. I'm the one who brings the tools onto the farm. Every time I save the farm an hour with a new gadget, I'm asking myself whose hour it was.

headlineQuote: Every time I save the farm an hour with a new gadget, I'm asking myself whose hour it was.
portrait: Priya is the **field and livestock lead** at Oakfield, an organic farm owned by a land trust.
She uses **AI every day** and enjoys change, so a no-change world bores her.
Her partner Leo is a **software tester**, which makes the household exposed sooner than her own job.
In the fast AGI picture she is **alarmed** for both incomes; with more warning she plans to **run the robots**.
She wants the trust and the public to **own the machines** and share the gains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Leo and Priya both changing jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that starts before people are out of work.
Rules letting the trust **own its robots** instead of renting them.
